newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Debate still seen on Australia labour reform.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Debate still seen on Australia labour reform.

text.p: The political deal that secures passage of Australia's new industrial system had not brought forward the expected time the bill would become law, the Australian Democrats said on Monday.

The Democrats, whose backing has guaranteed passage of the Workplace Relations bill in an amended form, still expected a lengthy debate in the upper house of parliament, the Senate, Democrats spokeswoman Cheryl Thurlow told Reuters.
But the Democrats' agreement with the government for 171 amendments to the bill meant the changes would be passed by Christmas, as always expected, she said.
"The agreement that we've reached with the government certainly doesn't preclude significant debate in the Senate," Thurlow said.
"We are anticipating that it will be a long debate, but we think that's quite fair."
She said the opposition Labor Party and the Greens also had amendments that would be debated in the Senate.

"But in terms of many amendments that Labor have put forward, and the Greens for that matter, we actually think that we took consideration of those views in our discussions with the government," she said.
"We actually think that the agreement covers a lot of them."
Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith announced on Sunday that he had reached agreement with the Democrats for 171 amendments to the bill.
He said the changes, accepted after 52 hours of negotiations, maintained the "basic integrity" of the reforms promised at the March 2 election.
As a result, he expected Australia would have a new industrial relations system by February 1 next year.
Australia will move towards a more deregulated labour market under the reforms, with unions playing a less significant role in the wage negotiating process.

The government needed the support of the Democrats in order to pass the legislation in the Senate, where it does not have a clear majority and given the stated or implied position of other non-government Senators.
